question.prompt: Should assurance later add a dedicated journey that starts with no submissions in the current browser session and checks only the `/my-submissions` empty state and browse-packages link?

options.label: Keep deferred
options.detail: Keep the current 3-pair budget focused on submission visibility, withdrawal, and cross-session isolation.

options.label: Add if budget grows
options.detail: Raise coverage beyond 3 pairs later and mint a dedicated empty-state scenario and test.

content.risk_rationale: Useful but lower value under the 3-pair budget because the empty-state outcome is partially observable again after withdrawing the only submission, so a dedicated empty-state-only journey adds less incremental risk reduction.

content.title: Withdraw the only tracked submission and restore the shared package seat count
content.intent: Prove that withdrawing the current session's only tracked submission removes it from `/my-submissions`, returns one seat to the package's shared monthly pool, and leaves the session with no tracked submissions.
content.technique_notes: Techniques: equivalence partitioning + state / flow + CRUD round-trip. I used the representative tracked state of exactly one current-session submission because the source promises one-row withdrawal behavior and a one-seat restoration delta on the shared `/publish` pool. No covering array was needed because this journey has no independent multi-input interaction to combine; the risk-judged default strength would be 2 because no money, auth, or data-loss factor applies to this use-case.

content.title: A submission created in one browser session is not shown in a different browser session
content.intent: Prove that submission tracking is isolated to the browser session that created the submission, so a different browser session does not display that submission on `/my-submissions`.
content.technique_notes: Techniques: equivalence partitioning + negative / error + state / flow. I used two outcome-changing session partitions — the browser session that created the submission and a different browser session — because the source makes browser-session scoping an explicit visibility rule. No covering array was needed because there is one interaction axis; the risk-judged default strength would be 2 because no money, auth, or data-loss factor applies to this use-case.

content.title: View a newly created submission in the current browser session
content.intent: Prove that after a successful submission, `/my-submissions` shows the submission in the current browser session with the required table columns, `Under Review` status, matching header count, and per-row `Withdraw` control.
content.technique_notes: Techniques: equivalence partitioning + state / flow + CRUD round-trip. I used the representative transition from one successful submission to its first tracking view because the source promises one post-submit listing outcome with fixed columns, status, count alignment, and row action. No covering array was needed because there is no independent multi-input interaction to combine; the risk-judged default strength would be 2 because no money, auth, or data-loss factor applies to this use-case.

judgements.rationale: [value_score] Scored highest because withdrawing a submission mutates shared monthly seat capacity for all visitors and must remove the row correctly in the current session.
[value_score] Scored next because browser-session isolation is an explicit product promise and a leak would expose another session's submission data.
[value_score] Scored third because the first post-submit tracking view proves the required fields, status, count alignment, and withdraw affordance that anchor the rest of the feature.
[value_score] Scored lowest because a dedicated empty-state-only journey adds less incremental coverage once the withdrawal journey already returns the session to no submissions.
[applicability] Did not apply auth-gated techniques because the source states, `There is no sign-in anywhere on this platform. Identity is the browser session cookie, nothing more.`

[applicability] Did not mint new field-validation journeys here because data-entry validation belongs to the submission-creation use-case and is already represented by the dependency on the committed submission scenario.
[applicability] Did not apply search/list pagination or filtering techniques because `/my-submissions` is only promised as a simple table with no search, sort, filter, or pagination behavior.
